512.title: About my Father's business (Luke 2:41–52)
512.hook: he grew in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and people
512.howItsDone: Some Christians read Luke 2:52 as a picture of whole-person growth, and the finding in the temple is remembered as one of the five Joyful Mysteries of the Catholic rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anna, who prayed night and day and told everyone who was waiting. Your line was she never stopped.

A whole day's walk out of Jerusalem, Mary and Joseph realize their son isn't with them. They supposed him to be in the company, Luke says, traveling home from the Passover with relatives and friends. So nobody worried, until they looked among the kinsfolk and acquaintance, and he wasn't there. A parent who has lost sight of a child at a mall or a beach knows that cold drop in the stomach. They turn back and search the city. One day. Two days. On the third day they find him, and Luke tells us exactly where.
screen: `A DAY'S WALK, AND HE'S NOT THERE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, "after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, scholars of the law. And notice the order: hearing first, then asking. Mary speaks first: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." He answers with the first words Luke ever gives him: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" The Greek is shorter, something like in the things of my Father, and some translations say in my Father's house. Either way, he names God as Father, while Joseph stands right there. Luke adds, honestly, that his parents didn't understand. Then he goes home with them to Nazareth, and Luke says he was subject unto them: the boy who knew whose house he was in still does as his parents ask. Then the verse that closes the chapter: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." Christians believe Jesus was the Son of God, and Luke still says he grew: in learning, in height, in the trust of the people around him. Luke writes the growing down as part of the story. And Mary "kept all these sayings in her heart." She didn't understand yet. She kept it anyway.
screen: then, large: `JESUS INCREASED IN WISDOM AND STATURE.`

segments.voice: Picture the boy in the temple, listening among people who knew more than he did, and then the four ways Luke says he grew: wisdom, stature, favor with God, favor with people. Let one rise to the top for you, something to understand better, your body or your sleep, your prayer or your quiet, a relationship that could be kinder, and choose the smallest possible step in it. If you pray, ask to grow the way Luke says Jesus grew; if not, simply choose your step.
Wist. An old word for knew, from Jesus' first recorded words: wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?
Your line: growing is holy. Even Luke's Jesus increased, a little at a time. See you tomorrow.

513.title: What shall we do? (Luke 3:1–14)
513.hook: John tells the crowds: share your coat, don't cheat, don't extort
513.howItsDone: In the Revised Common Lectionary, John's preaching from Luke 3 is read in Advent, and some Christian charities point to Luke 3:11 for coat drives and clothing closets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wist ye not: a boy about his Father's business, who went home and grew. Your line was growing is holy.

Luke opens this chapter like a news anchor reading the date. The fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governing Judea. Herod ruling Galilee. His brother Philip, another ruler named Lysanias, the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Seven powerful names, the people with palaces and armies and seals. Then the sentence lands somewhere else entirely: "the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness." Not to the emperor. Not to the palace. To the son of an old priest, out in the empty country by the Jordan. And the crowds start walking out to hear him.
screen: `THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: John doesn't flatter them: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" Don't lean on your family tree, he says; the axe is already at the root of the trees. "Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." Repentance: a turn in how you live. And the crowd asks the honest question: "What shall we do then?" Here's the surprise. John doesn't tell them to move to the wilderness or give up their trades. His answers are almost ordinary. To everyone: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise." The coat is the everyday tunic. If you have a spare, someone else is cold. Tax collectors come to be baptized: "Master, what shall we do?" He doesn't tell them to quit: "Exact no more than that which is appointed you." Collect what's owed. Don't pad the bill. Then soldiers, men with weapons and power over civilians: "And what shall we do?" "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." Three groups, three answers, each fitting the person's actual job. In Luke, turning around doesn't start in a temple or a monastery. It starts at the closet, the tax booth and the checkpoint: at your own counter, with your own receipts.
screen: then, large: `WHAT SHALL WE DO THEN?`

segments.voice: Ask John's question about your own week: what shall I do? Walk through the places where money or time changes hands, a bill, a tip, hours logged, a price you set, a favor never paid back, and let one small place come up where you could be a little more honest or more generous than you need to be. Don't make it dramatic; John didn't. If you pray, ask the crowd's question and listen; if not, simply name that one place.
Chiton, the Greek word for tunic, the garment worn next to the skin: the coat John tells the crowd to share, alongside his plain answers for tax collectors and soldiers too.
Your line: share your coat. Small, fair and ordinary: that's where the turn begins. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: Son of Adam (Luke 3:15–38)
514.hook: after the baptism, Luke traces Jesus back past Abraham, to Adam, son of God
514.carry: son of adam, son of god
514.howItsDone: Some churches read Luke's account of the baptism on the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, and some Christians point to Luke's genealogy as a sign that Jesus belongs to the whole human family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chiton, and John's plain answers to what shall we do. Your line was share your coat.

Luke's family tree runs the wrong way. A family tree usually starts with the oldest name and works down. Luke starts with Jesus, about thirty years old, and climbs. Son of Joseph, as was supposed. Son of Heli. Son of Matthat. Back through King David, back through Abraham, back past the flood to Noah, and still he keeps going. A long ladder of fathers, easy to skip. But read to the very last rung, because of where Luke puts this list, and the strange, beautiful word he ends on.

People wonder if John might be the Christ, and he says no: "I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose." Then Jesus is baptized, and Luke adds that he was praying. "The heaven was opened, And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased." The voice has just said: my Son. And right there, Luke drops in the genealogy. Matthew's begins with Abraham and runs forward, a story of Israel's kings. Luke's runs backward and doesn't stop at Abraham. It ends: "Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God." In Genesis, Adam is also the name God gives humankind, male and female together. So some readers hear Luke tying Jesus to every person who has ever lived, the whole human family. And Adam is called a son of God too. The voice at the river says this one is my beloved Son; the list underneath says he belongs to everyone. Between David and Joseph the two lists don't match name for name, and Christians explain that differently: some say Luke follows Mary's family, others point to adoption or old family custom. The texts don't say. What Luke makes plain is the shape: from the river all the way back to the garden.
screen: then, large: `WHICH WAS THE SON OF ADAM, WHICH WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Start with your parents, or whoever raised you, then their parents, then one more step back, to names you've heard once, a village, an old photograph, or nothing at all. Picture them anyway, eight people, sixteen, who worked and worried and prayed or didn't, and keep going back past what anyone remembers, to the human family Luke traces. If you pray, give thanks for the ones whose names are lost; if not, simply notice how long the line is.
Adam, the name Genesis gives both the first man and all humankind, near the top of Luke's family tree.
Your line: son of adam, son of god. One family, all the way back. Until tomorrow.

515.title: The desert, Luke's way (Luke 4:1–13)
515.hook: full of the Spirit, led into the wilderness, and the devil leaves until an opportune time
515.howItsDone: Many churches read the temptation in the wilderness on the first Sunday of Lent, and the forty days of Lent are often linked to Jesus' forty days in the desert.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam: Luke's family tree climbing back to the son of God. Your line was son of adam, son of god.

Anyone who has quit something knows the dangerous moment isn't always the first day. It's day forty. You've made it. You're proud. You're tired. And then the old thing shows up, sounding perfectly reasonable. Luke's wilderness story begins, in the King James Bible: "Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness." Full of the Spirit, and led straight into the hardest place. Forty days without food. And Luke says, with almost comic plainness, "when they were ended, he afterward hungered." That's when the voice arrives.
screen: `FULL OF THE SPIRIT, LED INTO THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: The devil makes three offers, each aimed at something real. First, hunger: "If thou be the Son of God, command this stone that it be made bread." Jesus answers from Deuteronomy: "It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." Second, power: all the kingdoms of the world, shown in a moment, if he will only worship. He refuses. Third, Luke takes him to Jerusalem, to a high point of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. This time the devil quotes scripture too, a psalm about angels bearing you up. Jesus answers: "It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Here's Luke's way. Matthew tells the same three tests but puts the mountain last. Luke puts Jerusalem last. That's no accident: Luke's whole Gospel walks toward Jerusalem. It opened there, with Zechariah in the temple, and it will end there. Then the line that gives today its name: "And when the devil had ended all the temptation, he departed from him for a season." The Greek is achri kairou, until an opportune time. Not gone forever. Just waiting. Readers often see that time return near the end, when Luke says Satan entered into Judas, and in the garden, where Jesus prays in agony. Christians have long read this as honest news: passing one test doesn't end the testing. Temptation keeps a calendar.
screen: then, large: `HE DEPARTED FROM HIM FOR A SEASON.`

segments.voice: Walk through an ordinary day in your mind and find your weakest hour, late at night with the phone, right after a hard meeting, hungry, tired, alone, bored, the way you'd find a weak board in a floor, without scolding yourself. Then picture one small thing set there ahead of time: a glass of water, a walk, a verse, a friend to text, the phone in another room. If you pray, name that hour to God; if not, simply name it to yourself.
The desert. In Luke, Jesus goes in full of the Spirit, answers three tests with scripture, and the devil leaves only until an opportune time.
Your line: until another time. Full of the Spirit, and still tested. Day five hundred fifteen, done.

516.title: The Nazareth manifesto (Luke 4:14–21)
516.hook: he unrolls Isaiah: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed
516.tomorrow: to the edge of the cliff
516.howItsDone: Some Christian groups working with the poor, prisoners and the sick point to Luke 4:18–19 as their charter, and in the Revised Common Lectionary the passage is read in the season after Epiphany.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert, where the devil left only until an opportune time. Your line was until another time.

A small-town synagogue on the sabbath. Everyone knows everyone. Today the young man who was brought up here, Joseph's son, is back, and word about him has spread through the region. Luke says he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, "as his custom was." He stands up to read. The attendant hands him a scroll, the prophet Isaiah. And Luke slows down for a detail: he unrolls it, looking for a particular place. He's choosing his words. Luke has said he was already teaching in synagogues, but this is the first time Luke lets us hear what he says.

He reads, in the King James words: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord." Count who's in it. The poor. The brokenhearted. The captives. The blind. The bruised, the crushed and oppressed. Five kinds of people, and not one of them powerful. That's why some readers call this the Nazareth manifesto: a mission statement, read out at the start. Some hear in the acceptable year of the Lord an echo of the jubilee in Leviticus, the fiftieth year, when liberty was proclaimed and land went back to its families. Then: "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Everyone waits. Then one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." Not someday, for those five kinds of people: now, in the room where they're sitting. And a quiet detail you can check: set Luke beside Isaiah 61, and he stops reading mid-verse, just before Isaiah's next words, the day of vengeance of our God. Christians read that pause in different ways, but it's there.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.`
`HE SAT DOWN; EVERY EYE ON HIM.`
then, large: `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED IN YOUR EARS.`

segments.voice: Let the five come back slowly, waiting a breath with each: the poor; the brokenhearted, grieving or lonely; the captive, stuck in debt, in prison, in a habit; the blind, who can't see a way forward; the bruised, pushed down by others. Notice if one of them has a face, someone you actually know or pass every week, and hold them there with care. If you pray, hold that person before God; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Jubilee. The Levitical year of liberty and land returned, echoed in the acceptable year of the Lord that Jesus read about himself.
Your line: today this is fulfilled. Good news for the five, not someday. See you tomorrow.

517.title: To the edge of the cliff (Luke 4:22–30)
517.hook: his own town loves him, then tries to throw him off a cliff, and he walks through them
517.howItsDone: Some Christians read the rejection at Nazareth as a picture of how hard it is to hear a prophet close to home, and Nazareth has a traditional hilltop site linked to the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jubilee: Isaiah's scroll, five kinds of people, and one word, today. Your line was today this is fulfilled.

"Is not this Joseph's son?" It's said in the same synagogue, a minute after the reading, and at first it sounds proud. Luke says they "wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth." The hometown boy, all grown up. You can almost hear the aunties. But hometowns are complicated. The same people who love you also think they know exactly who you are, and what you owe them. We've heard what you did in Capernaum, they're thinking. Do it here. Within a few verses, this warm room becomes a crowd marching him to the edge of a hill.

Jesus names what they're thinking: "Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself." Then: "Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country." And he reaches for two stories from their own scriptures. In the days of Elijah there was a famine, and many widows in Israel, but the prophet was sent to a widow in Sarepta, in the region of Sidon, outside Israel. In the days of Elisha there were many lepers in Israel, "and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian." A foreign widow. A foreign general. Both showing God's care reaching past the expected circle. That turns the room. "All they in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath," and it moves fast: they "thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong." This isn't about one town being worse than others. It's something any group can do: love the prophet until the prophet says God's kindness isn't only ours. Then the ending, so quiet you can miss it: "But he passing through the midst of them went his way." No miracle is described. No fight, no speech, no running. He walks through the crowd and keeps going. Luke doesn't explain how, and the silence is part of the picture: the anger doesn't get to decide his direction.

`FILLED WITH WRATH, TO THE BROW OF THE HILL.`
`THROUGH THE MIDST, AND ON HIS WAY.`
then, large: `HE PASSING THROUGH THE MIDST OF THEM WENT HIS WAY.`

Then picture Jesus at the brow of the hill, walking steadily through, no shouting, no pleading, and breathe slowly while your shoulders drop. If you pray, ask for that steadiness; if not, simply practice the slow breath.
Patris, Greek for homeland, hometown: his own town wonders at him, then turns on him, and he walks through the middle of them.
Your line: he went his way. Not fighting the crowd, and not obeying it. That's day five hundred seventeen.

518.title: Laying on hands (Luke 4:31–44)
518.hook: at sunset they bring the sick, and he lays his hands on every one
518.howItsDone: Churches lay hands on people in ordination, some in confirmation, and in prayer for the sick, including the Catholic and Orthodox anointing of the sick and healing prayer in Pentecostal and charismatic churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, patris: a hometown that turned, and a man who walked through the crowd. Your line was he went his way.

Capernaum, a city of Galilee. The day began on the sabbath, with Jesus teaching in the synagogue. Now the sun is going down, and the streets start to fill. Luke doesn't say why the crowd waits for sunset; some readers connect it with the sabbath, which ends at sundown. Mats, stretchers, people leaning on cousins' shoulders, children being carried. Everyone with someone sick is heading to the same door, the house of a man named Simon.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO GO DOWN.`

segments.voice: The day began in the synagogue, where a man possessed by an unclean spirit cried out, and Jesus said: "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." People were stunned: "What a word is this!" Then, at Simon's house, Simon's mother-in-law lay "taken with a great fever." Luke, whom tradition remembers as a physician, says Jesus "stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them." She gets up and serves the table. Then sunset, and the verse behind today's title: "Now when the sun was setting, all they that had any sick with divers diseases brought them unto him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them." Every one of them. Not a wave from the doorway, not a blessing in bulk. Hands on each person, one by one. Laying on hands was an old gesture in Israel's scriptures, for blessing and for setting someone apart. Christians kept it: in ordination, in confirmation in some churches, and in prayer for the sick, from Catholic and Orthodox anointing to Pentecostal healing services. Then, at dawn, Jesus slips away to a deserted place. The crowds find him and beg him to stay. He says: "I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also: for therefore am I sent." Full attention to each person at night. In the morning, he moves on, because, he says, that is what he was sent for.
screen: `THE FEVER LEFT; SHE ROSE AND SERVED.`
then, large: `HE LAID HIS HANDS ON EVERY ONE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Picture that doorway at sunset, the line of people, and one pair of hands, one person at a time. Then bring to mind someone who usually gets the half of you that's looking at a screen, a child, a partner, a parent on the phone, a coworker, and picture giving them all of you for five minutes: eyes up, phone away, listening to the end of their sentences. If you pray, hold that person before God; if not, hold them in mind with care.
Capernaum. The city where, at sunset, Jesus laid his hands on every sick person brought to Simon's door, one by one.
Your line: every one of them. A week of a boy in the temple, a crowd at the river, a desert, a hometown and a doorway at sunset. Seven days, done.

chat.says: When the sick crowded Simon's door, did Jesus just bless them all at once?
options: No, Luke says he laid his hands on every one of them, one by one.
Yes, he blessed them from the doorway, then went inside to rest.
No, he healed only Simon's family and sent the rest to the temple.
chat.meaning: "He laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them": not a blessing in bulk, but hands on each person, one at a time.
